actin–microtube coordination is mediated by a simple cross-linking protein, and that the distinct mechanical properties and organization of actin structures determine the outcome of acting–microtubue interactions.
growing microtubes can be guided by stiff actins and that microtubes can stretch and bundle individual filaments, thereby organizing actin.
actin filaments can be stretched and bundled by growing microtubular ends.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physical basis of cell motility and cell shape.
the mechanisms by which cells control and coordinate the actin and tubulin cytoskeletons.
how the actin and the microtubule networks in cells interact to generate complex structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TipAct, a protein that binds both actin and microtuobules, can act as a mechanical feedback mechanism between these two cytoskeletal elements.
the actin and tubulin cytoskeletons are highly dynamic and interconnected, and the coordination between them is vital for cell functions
the actin and tubulin cytoskeletons can influence the behavior of the other, and that this influence depends on the architecture of the actin filaments or microtubules.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we engineered a simple protein that can coordinate the actin and tubulin cytoskeleton.
we have shown how actin filaments can organize microtubules, and how microtubules organize actin filaments.
actin–microtube cross-talk can be achieved via a simple cross-linking protein that is able to couple the mechanical properties of actin and microtube filaments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
actin–microtu­bule cross-linkers are able to coordinate actin and tubulin polymerization.
actin filaments and microtubules are mechanically coupled by the actin–microtu­bule cross-linker TipAct.
the mechanical properties of the actin cytoskeleton can be used as an input to control microtubule dynamics and vice versa.
